title: Spatial Synchrony at the Extremes: Tail‐Dependence in Climate Drives Tail‐Dependence in Birds' Spatial Synchrony Across North America
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Understanding how climatic extremes influence species synchrony is crucial for predicting biodiversity responses to global change. We test whether spatial synchrony in bird abundances exhibits “synchrony at the extremes” (tail-dependence), whereby populations synchronize more strongly during unusually low or high abundance events, and whether spatial synchrony in climatic extremes and dispersal traits explain these patterns.

Location

North America.

Time Period

1979–2019.

Major Taxa Studied

Breeding birds.

Methods

We quantified spatial synchrony in bird abundance and climate (temperature and precipitation) using correlation- and tail-dependence-based approaches across sites separated by ≤ 250 km. Analyses were conducted for species monitored for ≥ 40 years (173 species), ≥ 36 years (276 species) and ≥ 32 years (328 species). We tested whether total and directional tail-dependent climatic synchrony predicted corresponding abundance synchrony using phylogenetic regression, with hand-wing index (HWI) as a proxy for dispersal ability.

Results

Across all temporal thresholds, 45%–73% of species exhibited significant spatial synchrony, of which 44%–52% also exhibited significant tail-dependent synchrony (20%–38% of all species). In phylogenetic regression models, total tail-dependent synchrony in precipitation consistently predicted total tail-dependent synchrony in abundance across all temporal thresholds (≥ 32, ≥ 36 and ≥ 40 years), whereas total tail-dependent synchrony in temperature was a significant factor only for the ≥ 32-year dataset. These models explained up to 24% of the variation, while HWI showed little evidence of an association. Support for the climate-abundance relationship weakened when analyses were restricted to narrower spatial distance classes. Directional tail-dependent synchrony in climate and HWI showed limited support for explaining directional tail-dependent synchrony in abundance.

Main Conclusions

Our findings demonstrate that synchronized climatic extremes, particularly in precipitation, are associated with synchronized bird population extremes across large spatial scales. Incorporating tail dependence into studies of spatial synchrony may improve our understanding of ecological responses to increasingly frequent climatic extremes.
